critique.paragraph: The map reads as an interactive control panel operating on a separate simulation, not as an apparatus that constitutively makes the phenomenon it measures. Edge H requires the apparatus and the phenomenon to be visibly the same thing — 'the path is the apparatus' — but here the sliders (apparatus) and reactor (phenomenon) are spatially and conceptually separate objects. From any angle, the wireframe reactor appears as static geometry being controlled, not as something being enacted by the act of observation. The visual grammar says 'parameter → response' (Edge C) rather than 'measurement makes the measured' (Edge H).
strengths: Central reactor is visually prominent and reads clearly from all angles
Particle systems provide visible responsive behavior
Spatial separation of control elements from simulation creates clear legibility
weaknesses: Apparatus (sliders) and phenomenon (reactor/particles) are separate objects, not constitutively entangled
No pathway-dependent reading — all elements visible simultaneously from above; no 'walk one path: wave, walk another: particle' grammar
Reactor appears as static wireframe geometry rather than something being made by measurement
Visual grammar reads as external control (sliders affect reactor) rather than observer-observed co-constitution
No visible indication that the learner's position or path enacts the apparatus cut
next_gen_hints: Make reactor form morph based on viewer position — west approach crystallizes it, east approach dissolves it; the path literally is the apparatus
Remove sliders entirely; let learner's spatial position (x,y on floor) implicitly set λ and φ — standing becomes measuring
Add three 'measurement stations' at different grid positions; standing at each station produces a different visual reading of the same central phenomenon (wave/particle/field)
Make particles trace visible beams from learner position to reactor — the observation ray is part of the diagram
Split reactor into two overlaid forms (crystalline + chaotic) with position-dependent opacity — apparatus-cut makes one real and other virtual
